stem: A parent asks why an immunocompetent 11-year-old who has never received HPV vaccine should start the series now. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: HPV vaccination is routinely recommended at age 11–12 years because it works best before exposure to HPV; when the series is started before age 15, most immunocompetent children receive 2 doses 6–12 months apart.
options.B: HPV vaccine is delayed until adulthood because vaccination is useful only after a person has already been exposed to HPV.
options.C: HPV vaccine treats existing HPV infection and therefore is given only after an HPV-related lesion or abnormal screening test develops.
options.D: HPV vaccination is recommended only for girls because HPV-related cancers do not meaningfully affect boys or men.

rationale: CDC recommends routine HPV vaccination at age 11 or 12 years, and vaccination may begin at age 9. The vaccine prevents new HPV infections and provides the greatest benefit when given before exposure. For people who initiate the series at ages 9–14 years and are not in a group requiring a 3-dose schedule, CDC recommends 2 doses at 0 and 6–12 months. HPV vaccination protects against HPV infections that cause cancers in both females and males and is preventive rather than treatment for an existing HPV infection or disease.
educational_objective: Explain the cancer-prevention purpose and routine schedule of HPV vaccination for an immunocompetent preteen, including why vaccination is given before likely HPV exposure.

source_claim_supported: CDC recommends routine HPV vaccination at age 11–12 years, permits starting at age 9, recommends a 2-dose series 6–12 months apart for most people who initiate before age 15, and states that the vaccine prevents new HPV infections and HPV-associated cancers rather than treating existing infection or disease.

correction_summary: Upgraded the original general cancer-prevention statement into a current CDC schedule and counseling scenario. Specified an immunocompetent 11-year-old with no prior HPV vaccine, added the correct 2-dose 6–12-month schedule for initiation before age 15, and explicitly distinguished prevention of new infection from treatment of existing HPV disease while preserving cancer-prevention relevance across sexes.
audit_findings: Original item correctly linked HPV vaccination to cancer prevention but did not test current age-appropriate dosing or the preventive-versus-therapeutic distinction.
Fresh CDC verification supports routine vaccination at age 11–12, initiation as early as age 9, and a 2-dose schedule when initiated before age 15 in most immunocompetent persons.
The stem specifies immunocompetent status to exclude the CDC 3-dose schedule required for certain immunocompromising conditions.
The final item explicitly rejects the misconception that HPV vaccination treats existing infection and the misconception that vaccination benefits only females.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct response with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, schedule error, or unresolved source conflict.
